lesson.title: Loop Patterns: Recognizable Shapes of Repetition
lesson.summary: Loop patterns are common, reusable structures, like searching, counting, and accumulating, that reappear across many unrelated problems once you learn to see the shape underneath the specific task.
lesson.body:
After writing enough loops, a useful thing starts to happen: instead of designing every new loop completely from scratch, you begin recognizing that many problems are really the same small number of shapes wearing different clothes. These recurring shapes are loop patterns, and they function as lightweight, reusable algorithms, small enough to hold entirely in your head, general enough to apply across countless specific tasks. A search pattern loops through items and uses break the moment a match is finally found. A counting pattern loops through items and increments a counter whenever some condition happens to be true. An accumulation pattern, covered in full detail next, loops through items and builds up a single combined result gradually as it goes.

Here is the counting pattern in action:
words = ["cat", "dog", "cat", "bird", "cat"]
cat_count = 0
for word in words:
    if word == "cat":
        cat_count += 1
print(cat_count)
Trace it word by word carefully. word is "cat": the condition is True, so cat_count becomes 1. word is "dog": the condition is False, so cat_count stays at 1. word is "cat" again: True once more, cat_count becomes 2. word is "bird": False, unchanged. word is "cat" one last time: True, cat_count becomes 3. After the loop finishes, cat_count is 3, and that final value is what gets printed. Notice how little of this code is actually specific to counting cats: swap the comparison and this exact same skeleton counts votes, counts failing test scores, or counts anything else at all that matches some condition.

The search pattern reuses the break statement covered earlier, stopping as soon as a match turns up rather than needlessly checking every remaining item, and the accumulation pattern reuses augmented assignment to build up sums, products, or combined strings one item at a time as the loop progresses.

The real payoff of learning these patterns well is speed of recognition when facing something new. When you encounter an unfamiliar problem, "count how many students passed" or "find the first negative number in this list," you don't need to invent a solution from first principles every time; you recognize it as a counting problem or a search problem whose general shape you have already solved before, and you can adapt a familiar skeleton rather than starting from a completely blank page.

None of this requires any new syntax beyond what loops already offer you. A loop pattern is simply a disciplined, well-tested way of choosing what to initialize before the loop begins and what to actually do inside its body, turning the general idea of "repeat this block" into a small, dependable toolkit for entire categories of problems you will meet again and again throughout your work as a programmer, long after any single specific example has been forgotten.
